in_text_mentions: are the metaphyseal blanch sign of Steel [22] and Klein's line [11]. The metaphyseal blanch sign of Steel is a radiographic double density seen on the anteroposterior view at the level of the metaphysis; this double density reflects the posterior cortical lip of the epiphysis as it is beginning to slip posteriorly and is radiographically superimposed upon the metaphyseal density. Klein's line is drawn along the anterior or superior aspect of the femoral neck; the epiphysis should normally intersect this line. In an early SCFE the epiphysis will be flush with or even below this line (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A is the left image, the AP view of bilateral hips in a 6-year-old female. The caption and in-text state the radiographs are consistent with right SCFE and possible left SCFE; the visible red dotted Klein lines not intersecting the femoral heads are a direct radiographic SCFE sign. The coarsened trabeculae, osteopenia, physeal widening and iliac crest irregularity are nonspecific metabolic/endocrine bone findings and are not used to reassign the panel to pseudohypoparathyroidism. B: Panel B is the right image, the frog-leg view of bilateral hips in the same 6-year-old patient. The caption explicitly describes posteromedial translation of the proximal femoral epiphysis relative to the metaphysis, and the in-text states the frog-leg radiographs showed findings consistent with right SCFE with possible left SCFE. Additional metabolic-looking bone changes are noted as proposed findings only; the captioned slip establishes SCFE for this panel.

No specific subtype (stable/unstable, acute/chronic, grade) is stated, so subtype is null.

panels.rationale: Single coronal preoperative MRI T2 of the pelvis in a five-year-old diagnosed with stable SCFE. The solid arrow marks bone marrow edema surrounding the right physis, a direct MRI manifestation of SCFE matching the vocabulary finding transphyseal marrow edema; the dotted arrow indicates the contralateral left hip with no pre-slip findings. Disease attribution is supported by the article title, in-text mention ('diagnosed with stable SCFE'), and the specific captioned manifestation. Presentation in a 5-year-old is a recognized but less common form, hence variant. No skin is shown, and no ethnicity is stated. [raw subtype: stable]

in_text_mentions: external rotation, 75°/75°. Drehmann’s sign was positive on the right. She did not have previous history of trauma. No abnormalities or signs of an endocrine disorder were observed in the laboratory tests. Plain X-rays showed widening and irregularity of the physis of the right proximal femur, and the posterior sloping angle (PSA) was 35° on the right and 3° on the left (Figure 1). MRI showed obvious bone marrow edema surrounding the right physis but there were no findings suggesting pre-slip on the left (Figure 2). Despite the very young age of onset [10], she was diagnosed with stable SCFE.
